historical_claims.anchor: A classical extension is epistasis, in which variation at one locus alters or masks the effect of variation at another.
One gene can influence many traits, a phenomenon called pleiotropy.
Geneticists call the probability that a particular genotype produces a specified phenotype its penetrance.
In mammals with more than one X chromosome, X-chromosome inactivation produces cellular mosaics in which different cells may use different X-linked alleles.
Many genes can contribute to one trait.
Heritability is a population-level statement about variation under specified circumstances.
Twin and family studies provide one approach to estimating genetic contributions to variation, though they rely on assumptions about shared environments and family resemblance.
Such analyses are called genome-wide association studies, or G W A S.

A large study of human height published in 2022 analyzed data from about five point four million individuals and reported more than twelve thousand statistically independent association signals across thousands of genomic regions.
Statistical correction for ancestry and study design can reduce such confounding, but no single procedure automatically solves every problem.
Polygenic scores combine the estimated effects of many variants into a statistical index.
A score may shift the estimated probability of an outcome without being useful as a stand-alone decision,

description: Uses penetrance, epistasis, quantitative traits, heritability and genome-wide association to show why genotype does not translate directly into a simple trait.
